lines.narration: A crew-cut American kid knocks at a lantern-lit sliding door, and the greying man who answers says he expected him tomorrow — blaming the date his mother gave, Japan being a day ahead.
A young Japanese woman slips out behind him, takes her coat, and edges past the boy into the alley. The man drops his eyes. Caught out — and both of them know it.
Inside the cramped one-room flat he lays it out plain: this stay was the only thing standing between Sean and juvenile hall, and you cannot keep running every time trouble finds you.
The rules he settled with Sean's mother are three. Go to school. Come straight back here. And he does not want to see or hear about the boy anywhere near a car.
Next morning the man is gone, leaving an alarm clock, a black school uniform on a hanger, and a handwritten note. Everything a boy needs to start over, and nothing he wants.
Buttoned into that uniform, map in hand, Sean drowns in the Shibuya rush — shoved onto the wrong train, his bag pinned in a closing door. He reaches the gates long after the bell.
He walks into the lesson late and hands over his transfer paper. The class works him over for standing there in street shoes — so he just helps himself to a pair of slippers from the cubbies.
At lunch a student in a white headwrap introduces himself as Twinkie and immediately tries to sell him a laptop — sixty percent off, army brats and all.

claim.subject: the student in the white headwrap

lines.narration: Sean waves it all off — no cash, not an army brat, and probably not here long enough to remember the name. It is the line he keeps reaching for. Watch how long it survives Tokyo.
Then he clocks the racing steering wheel lying on the table. One of a kind, Twinkie brags. Sean's answer is two words: show me — the first thing in Japan he has actually wanted.

claim.subject: the student in the white headwrap

lines.narration: The automated lift delivers the one-of-a-kind ride: a bright green minivan painted like the Hulk, with a monster toy propped in the driver's seat. Sean mocks it all the way through the wash bay.
An attendant waves the van past a yellow barrier into an underground garage, and the mocking stops. Hoods up, nitrous bottles, a DJ, dancers — a whole tuner world humming under the city.
He follows the girl from his class to a teal car and leans in over the open hatch. She recognises him from the slipper stunt. Neela, he gets it right, and she tells him he is a quick learner.
He asks where she is really from — not where she lives, where she came from. Her smile holds, but her eyes drift off past his shoulder, and the question just trails away into the noise.
Whatever she was looking at, here it comes. A spiky-haired man in black leather rises from his seat and moves the meet with his crew, collecting cash and phones. The garage answers to him.

claim.subject: the man in the black leather jacket

lines.narration: He fronts Sean with the crew at his back, pulls Neela cheek to cheek to needle him, and calls him gaijin — outsider. This isn't your scene. His name is Takashi, and here that is a warning.
Sean, being Sean, pushes back — thought this was a free country, where a girl talks to whoever she wants. The crowd closes. Someone mutters the word Yakuza. Neela just tells him to leave.

claim.subject: the American in the grey tee
